title_zh: Rainwater 的 Joseph Shaposhnik 谈投资"可预测的生意"
description: Investing often comes down to making forecasts about an uncertain future, but some businesses are inherently more predictable than others. In this episode of Inside Active, host David Cohne, mutual fund and active management analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, speaks with Joseph Shaposhnik, portfolio manager of the Rainwater Equity ETF (RW), about his philosophy of investing exclusively in businesses with durable, recurring-revenue models. They discuss why predictability can be a competitive advantage, how free cash flow and disciplined capital allocation drive long-term value creation, and what separates exceptional management teams from the rest. They also explore how Shaposhnik identifies recurring-revenue businesses across industries, why avoiding negative surprises is as important as finding winners, and where he sees opportunities as investors continue to concentrate capital in AI-related companies. Recorded July 16.

turns.en: Welcome to Inside Active, a podcast about active managers, goes beyond sound bites and headlines and looks deeper into the processes, challenges, and philosophies and security selection. I'm David Cohne, i lead mutual fund and active Research at Bloomberg Intelligence. Investing often involves making forecasts about an uncertain future. Portfolio managers spend enormous amounts of time trying to predict earnings, economic conditions, competitive dynamics, and market sentiment. Yet for many businesses, those outcomes can change quickly, making even the best forecasts difficult to sustain. One way to reduce that uncertainty is to focus on companies whose businesses are inherently more predictable. Firms of occurring revenue, strong customer retention, discipline, capital allocation, and durable competitive advantages can provide investors with greater confidence and long term cash flows even as markets become more volatile. That doesn't eliminate risk, but it can change where investors choose to take it. Today, I wanted to explore what makes a business truly predictable, why recurring revenue is such an important part of the equation, and how those ideas translate into portfolio construction, security selection, and long term investing. So joining me to discuss that is Joseph Seposnic, portfolio manager of the Rainwater Equity ETF ticker RW. Joseph, thank you for joining me.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Inside Active，这是一档关于主动管理人（active manager）的播客。节目超越只言片语和新闻标题，深入探讨投资流程、挑战、投资理念（investment philosophy）与证券选择（security selection）。我是 David Cohne，负责 Bloomberg Intelligence 的共同基金（mutual fund）与主动管理研究。投资往往需要对不确定的未来作出预测。投资组合经理（portfolio manager）会花费大量时间，试图预测盈利、经济状况、竞争态势和市场情绪。然而，对许多企业而言，这些因素都可能迅速变化，导致即便是最出色的预测也难以持续有效。降低这种不确定性的一种方法，是专注于业务本身更具可预测性的公司。拥有经常性收入（recurring revenue）、较高客户留存率、严格资本配置（capital allocation）纪律和持久竞争优势（competitive advantage）的企业，即便市场波动率（volatility）上升，也能让投资者对长期现金流更有信心。这并不能消除风险，但可以改变投资者选择在哪些方面承担风险。今天，我想探讨一家企业怎样才算真正可预测，为什么经常性收入是其中如此重要的一环，以及这些理念如何落实到投资组合构建（portfolio construction）、证券选择和长期投资中。今天与我讨论这些话题的是 Rainwater Equity ETF（代码：RW）的投资组合经理 Joseph Shaposhnik。Joseph，感谢你参加节目。

turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。

turns.en: David, So you often say that most businesses can't be predicted. What led you to that conclusion and how's it shaped your entire investment philosophy.
turns.zh: Joseph，你经常说，大多数企业都无法预测。你为什么会得出这个结论？它又如何塑造了你的整个投资理念？

turns.en: Well, I want to take you back to my start in the industry. I started at Fidelity and I joined out of undergrad. I went to Berkeley for undergrad and I came to Boston and my boss said, you're from California, so you must know something about semiconductors. So they gave me research coverage of the semiconductor industry back in two thousand and five, small cap semiconductor businesses. Those businesses are not the businesses of today, which are great businesses with lots of customers, tremendous demand, and a very bright outlook for the future. Back then, they were very small companies with just a couple of customers, and they were kind of going in and out of business. And I had I had research coverage of these small, small companies and they were very unpredictable. I can remember I hosted a company of a I hosted a meeting with the CFO of a small chip company supplying chips to the flat tanel display market, and he was talking about how great his business was and how everything was going well, and they had they had approximately three customers at the time, So we had the meeting. A couple of days later, they reported quarterly results and the stock went down sixty percent in one day. And all I can say is I was very happy that I didn't recommend that business, but I was also shocked into paying attention and trying to understand what could make businesses not have that outcome occur, What could help me as an analyst understand the types of businesses that are susceptible to being crushed and broken in the way that company was crushed and broken just a couple of days after my meeting and update with the CFO. So I had research coverage of semiconductors at the time, and then I was given research coverage of software businesses a year or two later. I found those businesses to be somewhat better businesses and more predictable, but that memory always stuck with me. I joined TCW a couple of years after that, and I was given research coverage of another cyclical sector, the industrial or chemical sector, and I had to grapple with this same issues cyclicality cash flows that were all over the place, difficult to predict, sector and in market. In the course of studying businesses in the industrial space, I came across a Maverick CEO who transformed his traditional industrial company it was called Roper Industries now called Roper Technologies, from a traditional pumps and valves, meat and potato semi business into a business that had some recurring revenue healthcare associated with it. They acquired these businesses and then he took another step to acquiring a freight matching software business, so kind of a hybrid between industrials and software, and then progressively into software, transitioning this cyclical industrial business into a more recurring revenue software and services company. And that stock was one of the best performing businesses in the industrial sector for the time period that I'd covered industrials at tc WE, approximately eight years, eight years or ten years or something like that. So these experiences and my discussions with him really influenced my style as an analyst, and I began to gravitate to more predictable businesses. Oh you know, I think one other experience also was very certainly shaped me. I looked at performance of Nvidia in twenty twenty two, not that long ago, just four years ago, and in twenty twenty two, Nvidia's insiders sold several hundred million dollars worth of stock as the stock declined about fifty percent that year. They were coming off demand that was falling off on kind of an overbuild of the bitcoin complex, and so they were taking it. In twenty twenty two, one year later, and videos shares were up tenfold, tenfold. So management had been selling hundreds of millions of dollars of shares as the stock declined fifty percent in twenty two, and in twenty three the stock was up tenfold. The smartest management team in the world, or at least one of them, couldn't foresee where its stock would be just one year later. It was a reminder to me and to many others that this business is very difficult, and predicting where most businesses will be is a very very difficult approach. In twenty fifteen, taking all of my learnings as an analyst and my evolution as an investor. We launched a fund at TCW which focused on investing only in predictable businesses. We called it Predictable Growth Businesses, and over that nine year period of managing it, we found that this approach could generate really, really strong returns for investors and do that in a very risk controlled way. Our thesis was, if you invest in businesses where the business model itself is geared toward recurring revenue sources, management is more likely to manage this business in a way to where they can accurately match expenses to revenue and they can appropriately put together a capital structure for the business because they can kind of see where revenue and cash flows will be over the next couple of years. So inherently the business is less prone to being disrupted and it's less prone to having management mismanage expenses or the balance sheet. We also found that these businesses, because of their inherent characteristics, were easier for us to value. It was harder for us to screw up. Valuing businesses where you could see the cash flows over the next couple of years, you could more accurately forecast what the businesses should be valued at and they therefore make an investment conclusion. And so these businesses had these inherent advantages. I think that the last advantage that we identified is that recurring revenue businesses give the management team the ability to play offense in a way that most companies can't. When you know where your cash flows will be over the next couple of years, it gives you the confidence to make investment decisions in your business, maybe more aggressively, and to make inquisitions of synergistic businesses that can help you both improve the moat that you've that you've built with your company and maybe expand your moat into the future as well. So those were some of the advantages that we see with recurring revenue businesses. And you know, there was a an update to the famous Hendred Best in Binders study that came out a couple of days ago, which I think is also important to point out. Obviously it's a very famous study by Best in Binder And you know, a couple of the conclusions were, number one, four percent of all stocks generate all of the markets returns in excess of the of the of I think the tenure treasury. That's one of the interesting conclusions. But I think the second interesting conclusion is he looked at and I think we could post this of course, or share this with you. He looked at the stocks over the last one hundred years that had the highest cumulative returns compounded returns, and if you look at the top three, they happen to be Altria, Vulcan Materials in Kansas City, Southern All three businesses compounded at sixteen and a half percent, fourteen percent, and fourteen percent over very long stretches of time one hundred years, one hundred years, and ninety six years. And all three of these businesses have substantial amounts of recurring revenue associated with them. So it's an approach that I think has been tested over time, but there hasn't been a strategy that has exclusively focused on only investing in recurring revenue companies.
turns.zh: 我想先带你回顾一下我刚进入这个行业时的经历。我从 Fidelity 起步，本科毕业后就加入了那里。我本科就读于 Berkeley，后来来到 Boston。我的老板说：“你来自 California，那肯定懂一些半导体。”于是，他们在 2005 年让我负责半导体行业的研究覆盖，具体是小盘半导体企业。那些企业与今天的半导体公司不同。今天的公司业务出色，拥有大量客户、强劲需求，未来前景也非常光明。但在当时，它们都是规模很小的公司，只有两三个客户，时常徘徊在生死边缘。我负责研究这些很小、很小的公司，而它们极难预测。我记得，我曾主持过一次会议，参会的是一家小型芯片公司的首席财务官（CFO）。这家公司为平板显示器市场供应芯片。他当时谈到公司的业务有多么出色，一切进展得多么顺利，而当时他们大约只有三个客户。会议结束几天后，公司公布季度业绩，股价一天之内下跌了 60%。我只能说，我非常庆幸自己没有推荐这家公司，但这件事也给了我极大的震撼，迫使我认真关注并试图理解：怎样才能避免企业出现这种结果？作为分析师，我怎样才能看出哪些企业容易遭受重创、走向崩溃，就像那家公司在我与首席财务官会面并了解最新情况后短短几天内所经历的那样？当时我负责半导体研究，一两年后，我又开始负责软件企业的研究。我发现这些企业的质量稍好一些，也更可预测，但那段记忆始终萦绕在我心头。几年后我加入 TCW，又开始负责另一个周期性行业——工业或化工行业。我不得不应对同样的问题：周期性、四处波动的现金流、难以预测的行业和终端市场。研究工业领域企业的过程中，我遇到了一位特立独行的首席执行官。他改造了自己的传统工业公司——当时名为 Roper Industries，如今名为 Roper Technologies——将其从经营泵阀等传统基础工业业务的企业，转型为带有医疗保健相关经常性收入的企业。他们收购了这些业务，之后他又更进一步，收购了一家货运匹配软件企业，于是公司成为工业与软件的混合体；随后又逐步向软件领域深入，把这家周期性工业企业转变为一家经常性收入占比更高的软件与服务公司。在我于 TCW 覆盖工业板块的大约 8 年、8 年或10年左右时间里，这只股票是工业板块表现最好的企业之一。这些经历以及我与他的交流，确实影响了我的分析风格，我也开始越来越倾向于更可预测的企业。还有一段经历肯定也深刻塑造了我。就在不久前的 2022 年，也就是4年前，我观察了 Nvidia 的表现。2022 年，随着公司股价当年下跌约 50%，Nvidia 内部人士卖出了价值数亿美元的股票。此前，由于 Bitcoin 相关产业过度建设，需求正在回落，他们当时正承受这种影响。到了 2023 年，也就是1年后，Nvidia 的股价上涨了10倍，整整10倍。管理层曾在 2022 年股价下跌 50% 时出售价值数亿美元的股票，而 2023 年股价却上涨了10倍。世界上最聪明的管理团队——或者至少是其中之一——都无法预见自家股票仅仅1年后会处于什么位置。这再次提醒我，也提醒许多人，这门生意非常困难，而预测大多数企业未来会处于什么位置，是一种非常、非常困难的方法。2015 年，我们把我作为分析师积累的全部经验以及我作为投资者的演变融为一体，在 TCW 推出了一只只投资于可预测型企业（predictable businesses）的基金。我们称之为 Predictable Growth Businesses。在管理这只基金的9年里，我们发现，这种方法可以为投资者创造非常、非常强劲的回报，同时以一种高度控制风险的方式实现这一点。我们的投资论点（investment thesis）是：如果投资于商业模式本身以经常性收入来源为导向的企业，管理层就更有可能以一种能够准确匹配费用与收入的方式管理企业，也能为企业设计适当的资本结构，因为他们大致看得到未来几年的收入和现金流会处于什么水平。因此，这类企业本质上不太容易遭到颠覆，也不太容易因管理层错误管理费用或资产负债表而出问题。我们还发现，由于这些企业的内在特征，我们更容易对它们进行估值（valuation），也更不容易犯错。如果你能够看清未来几年的现金流，就可以更准确地预测企业应有的价值，进而得出投资结论。因此，这些企业具备这些内在优势。我认为，我们发现的最后一项优势是，经常性收入企业能让管理团队以多数公司无法做到的方式主动出击。当你知道未来几年的现金流大致会处于什么水平时，就会更有信心在企业内部作出投资决策，或许也会更加积极；同时还能收购具有协同效应的企业，既有助于强化公司已经建立的经济护城河（economic moat），也可能进一步拓展未来的护城河。这些就是我们看到的经常性收入企业的一部分优势。几天前，著名的 Hendrik Bessembinder 研究发布了更新，我认为这一点也很值得指出。这显然是 Bessembinder 一项非常著名的研究。其中有几个结论：第一，全部股票中有 4% 创造了市场相对于——我想是10年期美国国债——的全部超额回报（alpha）。这是一个很有意思的结论。第二个有意思的结论是，他研究了过去100年里累计复合回报最高的股票——我们当然可以把这项研究发布出来，或者与你分享。排名前三的恰好是 Altria、Vulcan Materials 和 Kansas City Southern。这三家企业在非常漫长的100年、100年和96年期间，分别实现了 16.5%、14% 和14%的复合回报。而这三家企业都有相当大一部分收入属于经常性收入。所以，我认为这种方法已经经受了时间检验，但此前还没有一种策略专门只投资经常性收入公司。

turns.en: So if we go deeper, how do you actually define recurring revenue? You know? In other words, you know what truly separates a recurring revenue from a company that just simply appears stable.
turns.zh: 如果再深入一些，你究竟如何定义经常性收入？换句话说，真正的经常性收入企业与仅仅看起来稳定的公司，到底有什么区别？

turns.en: We bucket recurring revenue businesses into two categories. Number one, the traditional subscription recurring revenue company. There's a subscription associated with their business. That would be a business like Bloomberg, business like Netflix, a software business that has substantial maintenance associated with the product. That's the traditional definition of what a recurring revenue business is. The second type of recurring revenue business is what we would describe it as transactional recurring and transactional recurring businesses would be a credit bureau where there are only three credit bureaus in the United States and all of the economic activity in the United States essentially goes through those three credit bureaus. It's transactional because alums will fluctuate based on economic activity, but it's recurring because there are only three pipes, and if you want to get an answer, you've got to go generally to two out of three every time, and sometimes three out of three to get a decision. You could think of the ratings agency businesses in the same way. You could think of the aftermarket aerospace parts industry as a similar analog. You sell the original equipment part to Boeing or air Bus, and then the plane flies for thirty years, and you're the sole source provider of the replacement part, so as activity keeps going over the years. The airlines, the airline operators and the airlines have to come to you for that specific part and they can't go anywhere else. Those are the the two categories of businesses that we focus on that can also take the form of local monopolies. Is you could think of the waste collection waste management businesses that have local monopolies as being very very recurring, revenue oriented businesses. And I think a great example on the aftermarket aerospace parts industry is if you think of a very basic part on a plane, The most basic part of the plane, I would say, is the seat belt, and the next time you're flying, if you flip open to the back of your seat belt, you'll see that the provider of the seat belt is a company called Amsafe. Amsafe has been making seatbelts for many, many decades, and it was acquired by a company that is in our portfolio called Transdime. You would think that a seatbelt is a pretty i don't know, regular part on a plane that you could replace pretty easily, not particularly expensive, but it happens to be because of the way we regulate air travel, quite a established position and one that is difficult. It is very difficult to replace am safe position in the seatbelt market. The reason for that is that the seat belt needs to be certified with the FAA, the seat belt with the type of seat or the seat manufacturer, of which there are a couple, they have to be certified in a system, and the seat the seat I'm sorry, the seat belt, the seat itself and the position of the seat on the plane also has to be certified as well. So the cost of re certifying a seat belt is incredibly high. So amsafe has a very strong position on planes and has the ability or has substantial pricing power because of the way we regulate parts on planes and travel today. So as you can imagine if you look at other parts on a plane, they are also to the extent that they are sole sourced and proprietary. They have really really strong long term businesses and very very strong pricing power and not surprisingly, very very strong recurring revenue for many, many years. That's the type of business and type of part that we really like.
turns.zh: 我们把经常性收入企业分为两类。第一类，是传统的订阅型经常性收入公司，其业务与订阅绑定。例如 Bloomberg、Netflix，以及产品附带大量维护服务的软件企业。这是经常性收入企业的传统定义。第二类经常性收入企业，我们称之为交易型经常性收入企业（transactional recurring revenue business）。信用局就是一个例子：美国只有三家信用局，而美国几乎所有经济活动都会经过这三家信用局。之所以称为“交易型”，是因为业务量会随经济活动而波动；之所以称为“经常性”，是因为管道只有三条。每次想获得结果，通常都必须去三家中的两家，有时甚至要去全部三家，才能作出决定。评级机构的业务也可以用同样的方式理解。航空航天售后零部件行业也是一个类似的例子。你先向 Boeing 或 Airbus 销售原始设备零部件，之后飞机会飞行30年，而你是替换零部件的独家供应商。因此，随着飞机年复一年持续运营，航空公司、飞机运营商都必须向你购买那个特定零部件，无法去别处采购。这就是我们专注的两类企业，而经常性收入也可能体现为地方垄断。垃圾收集和废弃物管理企业拥有地方垄断地位，也可以视为非常、非常偏向经常性收入的企业。关于航空航天售后零部件行业，我认为一个很好的例子，是飞机上非常基础的零部件。要说飞机上最基础的零部件，我会选安全带。下次坐飞机时，如果你把安全带翻到背面，就会看到安全带供应商是一家名为 AmSafe 的公司。AmSafe 已经生产安全带很多、很多年，后来被我们投资组合中的一家公司 TransDigm 收购。你可能会认为，安全带只是飞机上很普通的一个零部件，应该很容易替换，价格也不会特别高。但由于我们监管航空旅行的方式，它实际上拥有相当稳固的市场地位，要取代 AmSafe 在安全带市场中的位置非常困难。原因是，安全带必须得到美国联邦航空管理局（Federal Aviation Administration, FAA）的认证；安全带与特定类型的座椅或座椅制造商——这类制造商有几家——必须作为一个系统取得认证；此外，座椅——抱歉，是安全带、座椅本身以及座椅在飞机上的位置，也都必须经过认证。因此，重新认证安全带的成本高得惊人。所以，AmSafe 在飞机上拥有非常强的地位，并且由于当今飞机零部件和航空旅行的监管方式而拥有相当强的定价权（pricing power）。可以想见，如果考察飞机上的其他零部件，只要它们是独家供应且专有的，就会拥有非常、非常强劲的长期业务、非常强的定价权，而且毫不意外地会在很多、很多年里获得非常强劲的经常性收入。这就是我们真正喜欢的企业类型和零部件类型。

turns.en: So when you're finding these businesses, what other characteristics do you look at that basically have to be present before it makes it into your fund.
turns.zh: 那么，在寻找这些企业时，一家公司要进入你的基金，还必须具备哪些基本特征？

turns.en: Well, we only invest, as we talked about, in recurring revenue businesses that generate substantial free cash flow and have a dominant market position. The businesses have to be selling a critical part or service, critical product or service, so you won't see us invest in any discretionary businesses. Generally we avoid consumer facing businesses, and so we're trying to build this durable compounder of free cash flow that over time will create a snowball of free cash flow which physically moves the value of stocks and the underlying portfolio forward over time. Our view is that stocks are driven at the end of the day by the free cash flow that they generate, and our view of free cash flow is what physically moves stock prices. It isn't revenue, it isn't earnings, it's not but at the end of the day, it's the free cash flow that the company generates. And so we're looking for businesses that sell something that's very important to the customer, have very very few competitors, and generate substantial amounts of free cash flow. The second element of what we look for is we really believe that management is incredibly important. I remember when I was at Fidelity, it was strongly emphasized to us as young analysts to stay close to our companies, and we spend a lot of time talking to management. And what I've found over the years is that being aligned with great management is as important as being aligned with a great business. I found that bad management can ruin a great business, and that great management can enhance even an average business. So for us, when we think about management and assessing management, we're looking for a couple of key elements. And I think that these elements are relatively underappreciated because a lot of people say, oh, we look for great management. But for us, we go back to a quote that Warren Buffett gave in a talk that he gave to the University of Omaha, I think in the early eighties, where he said when he's when he's analyzing or assessing a management team, he said he's looking for one word, a fanatic. And when we assess management and management teams, we are looking for fanatics. Fanatics for us, I mean individuals or teams that are committed to their business. They're not just mercenaries. This business is a part of their life. It's a part of their psyche, it's a part of their makeup. And so when we meet with them, we're trying to understand is this business just something that they work on because it generates a nice stream of income for them, or is this business something that is really important to them and they are fanatical about it. One of the ways you can determine that is obviously looking at the track record, which we spend a lot of time looking at the track records of management teams, but we spend a lot of time meeting with them to try to understand that are they a fanatic. The second element that we look for, to the extent that we can determine that they are fanatics is do they have the right incentives in place to create shareholder value over time? And of course all management teams have incentives in place. Many management teams are highly compensated. But the question is is the compensation are the compensation metrics that have been laid out for the management team consistent with creating value for shareholders and for and for customers and and UH and for employees. And we find very often that the metrics that are laid out in the proxy really don't have a great deal of connection to creating shareholder value over time. In other words, there are very often UH in the types of businesses that we look for management is incentivized to grow revenue, maybe even to grow profit. But if there isn't a connection between growing revenue and generating higher returns on capital or compounding free cash flow over time, what you'll see is companies acquire revenue maybe in products which create revenue growth, but not a lot of profit or cash flow growth, and over time, those companies don't create as much value as companies that can link revenue, free cash flow, and returns together to create an incentive structure that incentivizes the management team to balance those elements and hopefully improve and grow them over time. And we think the growth of cash flow and return on invested capital and the top line is the combination that really is beneficial to the company and to shareholders. And the third element that we look for when we assess a management team is their capital allocation track record. Because we invest in these durable, recurring, revenue, cash generative companies, it's really important that the management teams have the capability of being great CEO investors, as we call them. Are they great investors because they're generating all of this cash flow and are they investing that well? You know, today a lot of people are asking that question of Microsoft, in Amazon, and Google, the great hyperscalers of our time. They generate enormous, enormous operating cash flow, and the management teams today are allocating that enormous sum of freak or operating cash flow to building out their presence in AI, their presence in the cloud. And the question is will those companies generate sufficient returns on the hundreds of billions of dollars of capex that they're investing in just this year. And so it's very important as we assess our management teams to be aligned with great investor management teams who have a capability have a track record and a capability of being able to reinvest the free cash or that they generate into projects or capital investments that will create more cash flow for investors over time. So that's generally what we're looking for in businesses. And then once we found these businesses, we like to hold on to the winners for a long period of time. We've found that there's a significant amount of persistence for winning stocks, and because of that, we try to hold on to these businesses for many, many years.
turns.zh: 正如我们谈到的，我们只投资能够产生大量自由现金流（free cash flow, FCF）并拥有主导市场地位的经常性收入企业。这些企业必须销售至关重要的零部件或服务、关键产品或服务，因此你不会看到我们投资任何可选消费型企业。总体而言，我们会避开面向消费者的企业。我们试图打造一个由自由现金流持久复利增长型公司（compounder）构成的组合，随着时间推移形成自由现金流雪球，从而实实在在地推动股票价值和底层投资组合价值长期向前。我们的观点是，归根结底，股票由其创造的自由现金流驱动。在我们看来，真正推动股价的是自由现金流。不是收入，不是盈利；归根结底，是公司创造的自由现金流。因此，我们寻找的是这样一些企业：它们向客户出售非常重要的产品或服务，竞争对手非常、非常少，同时能够产生大量自由现金流。我们考察的第二项要素是：我们坚信管理层极其重要。我记得自己在 Fidelity 时，公司会向我们这些年轻分析师反复强调，要与所覆盖的公司保持密切联系，我们也会花大量时间与管理层交流。多年来我发现，与优秀管理层利益一致，和投资一家优秀企业同样重要。我发现，糟糕的管理层可以毁掉一家优秀企业，而优秀的管理层甚至能改善一家普通企业。因此，在思考和评估管理层时，我们会寻找几个关键要素。我认为这些要素相对没有得到足够重视，因为很多人都会说：“哦，我们寻找优秀的管理层。”但对我们而言，我们会回到 Warren Buffett 在一次演讲中说过的一句话。那次演讲是他在20世纪80年代初——我记得是那个时候——面向 University of Omaha 所作的。他说，在分析或评估管理团队时，他寻找的是一个词：“狂热者。”我们评估管理层和管理团队时，寻找的正是狂热者。所谓狂热者，是指那些献身于自身事业的个人或团队。他们不只是雇佣兵。这家企业是他们生活的一部分，是他们精神世界的一部分，也是他们性格构成的一部分。因此，与他们会面时，我们试图了解：这家企业对他们而言，是否只是因为能够带来不错的收入而从事的一份工作，还是它对他们真的非常重要，他们也真的对它充满狂热？一种判断方法显然是考察过往记录；我们会花大量时间研究管理团队的过往记录，也会花很多时间与他们见面，试图判断他们是否真的是狂热者。在我们能够确定他们是狂热者的前提下，第二项要素是：他们是否建立了正确的激励机制，以便长期创造股东价值？当然，所有管理团队都有激励机制，许多管理团队也获得了很高的薪酬。但问题在于，为管理团队设定的薪酬指标，是否有助于为股东、客户和员工创造价值？我们经常发现，委托书中列出的指标与长期创造股东价值并没有太大关系。换句话说，在我们寻找的企业类型中，管理层往往会受到扩大收入的激励，甚至可能受到增加利润的激励。但如果扩大收入与提高资本回报率，或者长期实现自由现金流复合增长之间缺乏联系，你就会看到公司通过收购收入、也许通过收购产品来实现收入增长，但利润或现金流并没有增加多少。长期来看，这些公司创造的价值，不及那些能把收入、自由现金流和回报联系起来的公司。后一类公司能够建立一种激励结构，促使管理团队平衡这些要素，并有望让它们长期改善和增长。我们认为，现金流、投入资本回报率（return on invested capital, ROIC）和营业收入的共同增长，才是真正有利于公司和股东的组合。我们评估管理团队时考察的第三项要素，是他们的资本配置过往记录。由于我们投资的是这些持久、拥有经常性收入并能创造现金的公司，管理团队是否有能力成为我们所说的优秀“投资者型首席执行官”，就非常重要。他们创造了所有这些现金流，那么他们是不是优秀的投资者？能否把这些现金投资好？如今，许多人都在针对 Microsoft、Amazon 和 Google 提出这个问题——它们是我们这个时代伟大的超大规模云服务商。这些公司创造了极其庞大的经营现金流，而如今管理团队正把这笔巨额自由现金流或经营现金流，投入建设它们在人工智能（artificial intelligence, AI）和云计算领域的业务版图。问题是，仅今年它们就投入了数千亿美元的资本性支出，这些公司能否从中获得足够的回报？因此，在评估管理团队时，与优秀的投资型管理团队站在一起非常重要。这些团队应当有能力，也有过往记录证明，能够把公司创造的自由现金再投资于项目或资本投资，从而长期为投资者创造更多现金流。总体而言，这就是我们寻找的企业。找到这些企业后，我们希望长期持有赢家。我们发现，表现优异的股票具有相当显著的持续性，因此会努力持有这些企业很多、很多年。

turns.en: I do want to go back to cash flow for just a minute. You know, many growth managers focus on revenue growth. You know, you're obviously focusing on cash flow growth. Why do you think cashflow is actually, you know, ultimately the better north star in terms of growth.
turns.zh: 我确实想再回到现金流，简单谈一会儿。许多成长型管理人专注于收入增长，而你显然专注于现金流增长。为什么你认为，从增长的角度看，现金流最终才是更好的“北极星指标”？

turns.en: Well, I think that at the end of the day, the value of your business is the are the future cash flows that you will generate out into the out into perpetuity, discounted back to the present. I wouldn't place free cash flow as the driving factor for each business at different places in its maturation cycle. Obviously, early stage businesses must generate revenue and the cash flow hopefully will come over time. But for the types of businesses that we focus on, the companies I would say that have already won, they should be in the mode of generating cash flow and either returning that cash flow back to investors, which we generally don't favor, or doing something with that with that cash flow, which will be quite productive. I would also say that cash flow, unlike many of the other metrics that you cite revenues, EBITDA, earnings, adjusted earnings adjusted EBITDA, all of these adjusted adjusted metrics that management likes to put in front of us, cash flow is not adjusted. Cash Flow is just cash flow and It's one of the purer measures of how a business is performing and whether it's creating any value at all. Many businesses, or some businesses that don't generate much in the way of cash flow and don't generate much in the way of growth, you know, you kind of wonder what is going on there. But the businesses that do generate a lot of growth and generate a substantial matter of cash flow and reinvest that cash flow effectively are businesses that are going to create a lot of value for investors, particularly if they can continue to grow and make great investments with their capital.
turns.zh: 我认为，归根结底，一家企业的价值就是它未来直至永续所创造的现金流，再折现回当前时点。对于处于不同成熟周期阶段的企业，我不会都把自由现金流视为驱动因素。显然，早期企业必须先创造收入，现金流则有望随着时间推移而出现。但就我们专注的企业类型而言——也就是我所说的那些已经胜出的公司——它们应该已经进入创造现金流的阶段；它们要么把现金流返还给投资者，不过总体而言我们并不青睐这种做法，要么利用这些现金流做一些富有成效的事情。我还想说，与刚才提到的许多其他指标不同——收入、EBITDA、盈利、调整后盈利、调整后 EBITDA，以及管理层喜欢摆在我们面前的所有这些经过调整、再调整的指标——现金流并没有经过调整。现金流就是现金流。它是衡量企业经营表现以及企业是否创造了任何价值的较纯粹指标之一。许多企业，或者说有些企业，既创造不了多少现金流，也没有多少增长，你会不禁怀疑它们究竟在做什么。但那些能够实现大量增长、创造可观现金流，并有效再投资这些现金流的企业，将为投资者创造大量价值；如果它们还能继续增长，并利用资本作出出色投资，就更是如此。

turns.en: You know another thing, I note your website frequently mentions fewer surprises. Do you think or do you believe avoiding negative surprises is ultimately more important than finding the next big growth company.
turns.zh: 还有一点，我注意到你的网站经常提到“更少的意外”。你是否认为，或者说你是否相信，避免负面意外，最终比找到下一家大型成长公司更重要？

turns.en: I think they're both very, very important. When I was running the old fund, I talked about addition by subtraction. When we look back at, you know, our annual performance, we always think about, could we have made one less mistake that year? And if we had made one less mistake that year, you know, our performance would have been substantially improved. And so what we're trying to deliver for clients is a better better outcome relative to the to the broad market, with risks that are substantially lower than that of an investment in the broad market index. So because of that, we favor these businesses, which, in our experience, generate fewer surprises because they're inherently more predictable and more reliable. And they are generally managed by individuals and teams, which have incentives to constrain the animal spirit, influence or impulses that management teams can have, but also incentivize them to play offense and to grow the business. So hopefully they're not taking excessive with their recurring revenue company, but hopefully they're also incentivized to grow this business and therefore generate a more predictable outcome than most companies will over time.
turns.zh: 我认为两者都非常、非常重要。管理以前那只基金时，我谈过“做减法也能带来增益”。回顾每年的业绩时，我们总会思考：那一年能不能少犯一个错误？如果那一年少犯一个错误，我们的业绩就会得到显著改善。因此，我们试图为客户提供的结果，是以远低于投资广泛市场指数的风险，取得优于广泛市场的表现。正因如此，我们青睐这些企业。根据我们的经验，它们带来的意外更少，因为其本质上更可预测，也更可靠。管理这些企业的个人和团队，其激励机制通常能够约束管理团队可能出现的“动物精神”及冲动，同时也会激励他们主动出击、推动企业增长。因此，我们希望他们不会让经常性收入公司承担过度风险，同时也希望他们得到发展企业的激励，从而长期实现比大多数公司更可预测的结果。

turns.en: Okay, another thing that caught my eyes. You know, your willingness to hold meaningful cast positions when valuations aren't attractive. In today's investment world, you know, managers often feel pressure to stay fully invested. How difficult does it to have that patience?
turns.zh: 好，还有一件事引起了我的注意：当估值不具吸引力时，你愿意持有具有实质规模的现金头寸。如今在投资界，管理人往往会感受到保持满仓的压力。保持这种耐心有多难？

turns.en: Not particularly difficult. We stay very disciplined in looking for the types of businesses that we've historically invested in, and there are times when we see great opportunities, and there are times when we're in between opportunities, and there are times when there aren't a lot of opportunities. Today, we think that there are a substantial amount of opportunities in the recurring revenue area of the market, and valuations today are probably more attractive than they've been in the in the ten years I've been a portfolio manager and operating UH this strategy. So I think there's a lot of opportunity UH in this area of the market. And I think that because the the the AI cycle has captured the attention of so many market participants. What's happened is that the AI associated businesses and and beneficiaries of AI, so kind of tangential beneficiaries of AI, have have generated enormous amounts of earnings growth in the last couple of years and are projected to generate enormous amounts of earnings growth. And that has essentially created this giant move of capital from the more predictable, steady, eddy durable businesses to all the way over to all of these fast growing AI beneficiaries, and that's created a much lower multiple environment for these still durable recurring revenue businesses because all of the capital has rushed to the other side of the market, much like occurred in nineteen ninety nine, when all the capital rushed to one side of the market created lots of value and what people call the anti bubble side of the market. And I think I would not call the current market a bubble, but I would say that the dynamic of capital rushing to one end of the market that's generating a lot of earnings growth right now, but it's uncertain that that will continue, has created a lot of opportunity on the other end of the market'sctrum, and that has made us extremely excited.
turns.zh: 并不特别难。我们始终严守纪律，寻找自己历来投资的企业类型。有时我们会看到很好的机会，有时处于两个机会之间，有时则没有多少机会。如今，我们认为市场的经常性收入领域存在大量机会，而现在的估值可能比我担任投资组合经理并管理这一策略的10年中任何时候都更具吸引力。所以，我认为这个市场领域存在很多机会。我认为，由于 AI 周期吸引了如此多市场参与者的注意，AI 相关企业、AI 的受益企业以及在一定程度上间接受益于 AI 的企业，在过去几年创造了巨额盈利增长，而且预计还将创造巨额盈利增长。这基本上推动资本大规模撤离那些更可预测、稳健持久的企业，一路流向所有这些快速增长的 AI 受益企业。由于所有资本都涌向市场另一端，这些仍然持久的经常性收入企业所处的估值倍数（valuation multiple）环境变得低得多。这很像 1999 年发生的情形：所有资本都涌向市场的一侧，却在市场上人们所说的“反泡沫”一侧创造了大量价值。我不会把当前市场称为泡沫，但我想说，资本涌向市场一端的动态——这一端眼下正创造大量盈利增长，但这种增长能否持续仍不确定——已经在市场光谱的另一端创造了很多机会，而这令我们感到极其兴奋。

turns.en: So in your career, obviously you talked about at the beginning, you know, the different sectors you are covering. Is Rainwater fundamentally sector agnostic or are you finding recurring revenue businesses clustering in certain industries or sectors.
turns.zh: 纵观你的职业生涯，显然就像你一开始谈到的那样，你曾覆盖不同板块。Rainwater 从根本上说是不受行业限制的吗？还是说，你发现经常性收入企业会集中在某些行业或板块？

turns.en: It's both. It's sector agnostic, and we find a lot of clustering. We certainly can go across sectors, and we have, but there are sectors that we have historically found great opportunities in and they inherently have the combination of very very strong business model, very very strong recurring revenue moat and management teams that are really talented at maximizing the opportunity of that particular moat. And so for us, that happens to be in aerospace, where you have these really unusual regulatory barriers, and so we've invested in Gero Space, run by probably the greatest industrial CEO of our time, Larry Kulp, who built Danaher, and he's optimizing a really strong recurring revenue engine business. We've found other great businesses in the aftermarket aerospace parts part of the industry, but we've also invested in totally different parts of the market, like stock exchanges, which are basically a tolling business on economic activity. So we own the Tel Aviv stock Exchange, which we've owned now for a while and has probably been our best performer, and we view that as a royalty on economic activity on it for a particular country. In that country, that happens to be the only stock exchange that operates. Obviously, we have multiple stock exchanges in the US, and so that's an example of a transactional recurring revenue business. Clearly there actually there's both subscription and transaction. You pay subscription to be listed, and then you pay as transactions occur. So it's really a very very beautiful business. So you could think of the industrial sector certainly an area where overrepresented. You can think of some of the other attractive sectors aside from stock exchanges, waste management, as we talked about as a sector that we've liked, railroads, there's certainly a sector that we've liked. Certainly, the data analytics businesses like the credit bureaus have been businesses that we've liked, and all of them have the characteristics that fit this unique approach that we followed for a while.
turns.zh: 两者都是。我们不受行业限制，同时也确实发现了大量集中现象。我们当然可以跨板块投资，而且也这样做过；但在某些板块，我们历来能找到很好的机会。这些企业天然结合了非常、非常强劲的商业模式、由经常性收入构成的强大护城河，以及真正善于充分利用特定护城河所带来机会的管理团队。对我们而言，航空航天业就是这样的领域，因为那里存在非常独特的监管壁垒。因此，我们投资了 GE Aerospace。它由 Larry Culp 领导；他可能是我们这个时代最伟大的工业企业首席执行官，曾打造 Danaher，如今正在优化一项非常强劲、拥有经常性收入的发动机业务。我们在航空航天售后零部件行业的其他部分也发现了一些优秀企业，但也投资了市场中截然不同的领域，例如证券交易所；它们基本上是对经济活动收取通行费的业务。我们持有 Tel Aviv Stock Exchange，至今已经持有一段时间，它可能是我们表现最好的投资。我们把它看作针对特定国家经济活动收取的一种特许权使用费。在那个国家，它恰好是唯一运营的证券交易所。显然，美国有多家证券交易所，所以这是交易型经常性收入业务的一个例子。当然，准确地说，它既有订阅收入，也有交易收入。企业为挂牌上市支付订阅费，交易发生时再支付交易费用。因此，这确实是一项非常、非常漂亮的业务。所以，你可以把工业板块视为我们明显超配的领域。除证券交易所外，我们青睐的其他板块还包括刚才谈到的废弃物管理；铁路当然也是我们喜欢的板块。信用局等数据分析企业自然也是我们青睐的企业。它们都具备契合这套独特方法的特征，而我们采用这套方法已经有一段时间了。

turns.en: I just want to move on to valuation for a few minutes. You had mentioned the recurring revenue businesses make it easier to look at valuations. You know, I think a lot of investors worry about paying already or forty times earnings for quality compounders. How do you determine when a great business has become too expensive or you know? Or is it ever? Can they become too expensive?
turns.zh: 我想用几分钟转到估值问题上。你刚才提到，经常性收入企业更容易进行估值。我认为，很多投资者会担心，为优质复利增长型公司支付30倍或40倍市盈率（price-to-earnings ratio, P/E）已经太高。你如何判断一家优秀企业是否已经变得过于昂贵？或者说，它们会不会过于昂贵？

turns.en: Well? I think that the evidence of the last couple of years in the software industry points to the fact that they can become too expensive, and they can. They can also be a very paranoil like concern that they will be disrupted as they are expensive. So that has been a double whammy, uh to that end of the of the market. But certainly businesses can become too expensive, and we spend a lot of time thinking about that. Generally speaking, if a business is performing well, its management team is continuing to operate as as they said they would, particularly in the area of capital allocation, and the company's market position continues to be strong, we are reluctant to sell out the position purely on valuation. Now, if the valuation becomes extreme, we certainly would would reevaluate the business. But I think the other the other part of the equation or side of the coin is you're always thinking about whether this idea is better than your next best idea, and as you are making those trade outs, as we're making those trade offs, certainly valuation plays a role in helping us determine whether one opportunity is more attractive than the other. But generally speaking, we hang our hat on investing in the really, really durable business that we believe will keep compounding free cash flow, as opposed to hang our hat on a low evaluation in hopes that that will bail us out over time. Generally, we'll lean to the to the first type and less so to the second type. Though of course you're always looking for more value for your dollar and a lower valuation for every unit of compounding that you think you can get.
turns.zh: 这个嘛，我认为过去几年软件行业的证据表明，它们确实可能变得过于昂贵。而且，当它们价格高昂时，市场也可能产生一种近乎偏执的担忧，害怕它们会遭到颠覆。因此，市场的那一端遭遇了双重打击。但企业当然可能变得过于昂贵，我们也会花很多时间思考这个问题。总体而言，如果一家企业经营良好，管理团队继续按照承诺行事——尤其是在资本配置方面——而且公司的市场地位依然稳固，我们不会愿意仅仅因为估值就卖出整个仓位。当然，如果估值变得极端，我们肯定会重新评估这家企业。不过，这个等式的另一部分，或者说硬币的另一面，是你始终要思考：这个想法是否优于下一个最佳想法？当你进行这些调换、当我们作出这些权衡时，估值当然会发挥作用，帮助我们判断一个机会是否比另一个更具吸引力。但总体而言，我们立足于投资真正、真正持久，而且我们相信会继续实现自由现金流复合增长的企业；我们不会把希望寄托在低估值上，指望低估值最终把我们解救出来。总体上，我们更倾向于第一类，而较少倾向第二类。当然，你永远希望每一美元都获得更多价值，也希望为你预计能够获得的每一单位复合增长支付更低的估值。

turns.en: Okay, you know, if we have this conversation ten years from now, what would happen? What would have to happen for you to say that rain Water was a success? Is it, you know, outperforming or is there kind of a broader objective you're trying to achieve for your investors.
turns.zh: 好。如果我们10年后再进行这场对话，需要发生什么，你才会说 Rainwater 取得了成功？标准是跑赢市场，还是说你希望为投资者实现某种更广泛的目标？

turns.en: Well, our objective is to is to change the lives of our investors. So we have today, you know, over a thousand investors we believe in the fund, and hopefully we'll attract more investors, and our our mission is to generate really really strong returns for those investors, as we did in the prior fund, and do that while keeping them out of trouble and ensuring that we managed a portfolio in a responsible way that keeps risk under control. And if we can do that, we think that we can positively impact hopefully thousands and thousands of lives over time, which I think will be incredibly satisfying to all of us on the Rainwater team. It reminds me of the great Will Danoff, a portfolio manager of Contrafund at Fidelity, kept taped on his glass wall outside of his office for all of us analysts to see, and it was a letter that he received from a couple that had just had a newborn and had informed him that they'd started the new born's college fund and had invested in Contrafund in hopes of growing that college fund and preparing for the eventual college experience of their child. And I think about that all the time. And our responsibility is as investors is to do a great job on behalf of our clients. And so in ten years time, our goal is to change many, many thousands of lives and help those people live better lives and hopefully their children have their children live better lives. That I consider it would be a great success for the Rainwater Equity TF definitely.
turns.zh: 我们的目标是改变投资者的生活。据我们估计，如今这只基金拥有超过1,000名投资者，我们希望吸引更多投资者。我们的使命，是像此前那只基金一样，为这些投资者创造非常、非常强劲的回报，同时让他们远离麻烦，并确保我们以负责任的方式管理投资组合、控制风险。如果能够做到这一点，我们相信，随着时间推移，我们有望对成千上万人的生活产生积极影响。我认为，对 Rainwater 团队的所有人而言，这都会带来难以置信的满足感。这让我想起伟大的 Will Danoff。他是 Fidelity Contrafund 的投资组合经理。他曾在办公室外的玻璃墙上一直贴着一封信，让我们所有分析师都能看到。那是一对刚刚迎来新生儿的夫妇写给他的信。信中告诉他，他们已经为新生儿设立大学教育基金，并投资于 Contrafund，希望让这笔大学教育基金不断增长，为孩子最终进入大学做好准备。我一直都会想起这件事。作为投资者，我们的责任就是代表客户做好工作。因此，未来10年，我们的目标是改变成千上万人的生活，帮助他们过上更好的生活，也希望他们的孩子能过上更好的生活。如果能做到这一点，我肯定会把它视为 Rainwater Equity ETF 的巨大成功。

turns.en: And I just have one more question before I let you go. If an investor is listening today and you want them to remember just one thing about your investment philosophy, what would you hope it was.
turns.zh: 在结束之前，我还有最后一个问题。如果一位投资者今天正在收听，而你希望他只记住你投资理念中的一件事，你希望是哪一件？

turns.en: That's a great question. I think our fundamental belief is that most businesses can't easily be predicted, and therefore let's just invest in the segment of the market that can be predicted. And that segment of the market that we believe can be predicted are businesses that operate a recurring revenue a business model. It could be subscriptions, it could be transactional recurring, it could be a local monopoly. But those types of businesses over time can generate excess returns. And partnering the business model with the fanatic management team together creates a combination that we think is very very powerful and provides investors with an alternative to the broad market indexes which are heavily weighted to a single theme. Obviously he's been a very very powerful theme, but doesn't provide them with a whole lot of diversification. I like our approach because we believe it will generate strong returns over time, but it also presents investors with a way to diversify some of their capital from the broad market indexes that are very concentrated, and presents them with hopefully businesses that will experience fewer disappointments and hopefully solid results over a long period of time.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的问题。我认为，我们的根本信念是，大多数企业都无法轻易预测，因此，我们只投资于市场中可以预测的那一部分。我们认为可以预测的部分，就是采用经常性收入商业模式的企业。它可以是订阅型业务，可以是交易型经常性收入业务，也可以是地方垄断企业。但这些类型的企业能够长期创造超额回报。把这种商业模式与狂热的管理团队结合起来，会形成一种我们认为非常、非常强大的组合，也为投资者提供了广泛市场指数之外的另一种选择。广泛市场指数高度集中于单一主题。显然，AI 一直是一个非常、非常强劲的主题，但这种指数无法为投资者提供多少分散化（diversification）。我喜欢我们的方法，因为我们相信它能够长期创造强劲回报，同时也为投资者提供了一种途径，使他们能够从高度集中的广泛市场指数中分散一部分资本，并有望让他们投资于那些会经历更少失望、长期取得稳健业绩的企业。

turns.en: Well, unfortunately we need to end here, but this is great Joseph, thank you again for joining me today.
turns.zh: 很遗憾，我们必须在这里结束。不过，这场讨论非常精彩。Joseph，再次感谢你今天参加节目。

turns.en: Thanks for having me was so much fun, and.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。这次交流非常愉快。
